items.q: Does n8n have a built-in GoHighLevel integration?
items.a: Yes. n8n includes a node called HighLevel, after the company that makes GoHighLevel. n8n's documentation lists what it does: create, fetch, update and delete contacts, opportunities and tasks; book appointments; and return free slots from a GoHighLevel calendar. For any other part of HighLevel's API, the docs point to n8n's HTTP Request node, which can reuse the same credential. The node signs in with either an API key for HighLevel's version 1 API, which HighLevel no longer maintains, or OAuth2 for version 2, which requires an app created in a HighLevel developer account with Sub-Account distribution and scopes for locations, contacts, opportunities and users. HighLevel's API article lists OAuth as an Agency Pro feature, so on Starter or Unlimited confirm the app can connect first. The node acts on GoHighLevel rather than listening to it, so an n8n workflow that should start when something happens in GoHighLevel begins with n8n's Webhook trigger, fed by a GoHighLevel workflow's Webhook action.

items.q: How do I use a GoHighLevel private integration token in n8n?
items.a: Create the token in GoHighLevel, then call the API from n8n's HTTP Request node. HighLevel's help article places Private Integrations in settings, at agency or sub-account level, and says to switch the feature on under Labs if it does not appear. Give the integration a name, tick only the scopes the workflow needs and copy the token immediately, because GoHighLevel shows it only once. n8n's built-in HighLevel credential offers an API key or OAuth2, not this token, so the HTTP Request node sends it in the Authorization header, along with the Version header that HighLevel's examples include, to the version 2 endpoints. HighLevel recommends rotating each token every 90 days; its rotate-later option keeps the old token working for 7 days while you update n8n. Each agency and each sub-account can hold up to 20 tokens, though HighLevel's API article reserves agency-level keys for Agency Pro.

items.q: Can I send GoHighLevel data to n8n without paying for premium workflow steps?
items.a: In most setups, yes. HighLevel's list of premium workflow steps includes the Inbound Webhook trigger and the Custom Webhook action, but not the plain outbound Webhook action, which posts a contact's fields, plus appointment or opportunity details when the trigger relates to them, to any URL, including an n8n Webhook trigger. HighLevel's pricing guide also lists no charge for API requests, so n8n can write results back to GoHighLevel through the API without a premium step. Premium steps cost $0.01 a run once a sub-account has used its 100 free runs, an allowance granted once that never resets. They are worth paying for when a request needs authentication or custom headers, or when an outside system must start a GoHighLevel workflow directly. Messages are separate: a text or email that n8n triggers through GoHighLevel bills at the normal usage rates.

items.q: How many n8n executions does a GoHighLevel automation use?
items.a: One per workflow run, however many steps the n8n workflow contains. Each request that a GoHighLevel webhook sends to an n8n Webhook trigger counts as one execution, so a workflow fired by every new lead uses roughly as many executions a month as you get leads. Schedules count every time they fire: n8n's pricing FAQ estimates that a workflow running every 5 minutes uses about 8,600 to 8,900 executions a month, more than three times the 2,500 included in n8n Cloud's Starter plan. That makes webhooks from GoHighLevel a cheaper design than having n8n check GoHighLevel for changes on a timer. n8n does not count test runs from the editor, sub-workflows called by another workflow, error workflows, polls that find nothing new or webhook requests rejected before the workflow starts. On n8n Cloud, Starter includes 2,500 executions a month and Pro includes 10,000.

items.q: Can an agency use one n8n instance for all its GoHighLevel clients?
items.a: Yes, on a self-hosted instance, as long as clients never get into n8n itself. n8n's license FAQ, which covers self-hosted n8n rather than n8n Cloud, allows an agency to build, run and maintain workflows for clients on its own instance and to charge for that work, with no limit on the number of clients, provided clients receive only the results and cannot create or edit workflows. Hosting n8n so that clients build their own automations falls outside the free license and needs a commercial agreement with n8n. On the GoHighLevel side, Starter and Unlimited give location-level API access, so the agency should plan on a separate credential for each client sub-account, and HighLevel applies its rate limits per app and per sub-account. Plan the team side as well: on the free Community Edition, a workflow or credential is visible only to the instance owner and its creator, and sharing with colleagues needs a paid plan.

items.q: What happens when GoHighLevel or n8n usage goes past the plan's allowance?
items.a: GoHighLevel keeps running premium steps and bills them; n8n's answer depends on the plan. In GoHighLevel, each premium step in a sub-account without Workflow Pro costs $0.01 from the agency wallet once that sub-account's 100 free lifetime runs are gone. On a Workflow Pro tier, runs beyond the monthly allowance continue at that tier's overage rate, $0.008 a run on the $10 Starter tier, and HighLevel's article says workflows keep processing if the limit is reached mid-run. n8n's pricing FAQ says workflows on the Business and Enterprise plans keep running past their quota, n8n's sales team gets in touch as usage nears the limit, and overages are invoiced automatically 45 days later if there is no upgrade. The page does not say what happens on Cloud Starter or Pro, so track the execution count on n8n's Insights dashboard and move up a plan before a busy month.

items.q: Do I need a developer to connect GoHighLevel and n8n?
items.a: Not for the simplest flows, but budget for technical help once the API is involved. HighLevel's help article says the outbound Webhook action needs no coding, only a destination URL, which an n8n Webhook trigger provides. Writing back into GoHighLevel takes more work: n8n's OAuth2 credential for HighLevel requires creating an app in a HighLevel developer account, and the private integration token route means building HTTP requests against version 2 of HighLevel's API. HighLevel's support team does not help build or debug API integrations; its API article sends developers to the documentation, a developer Slack community and a bug-report form instead. On n8n's side, Cloud removes the server work, while self-hosting the free Community Edition adds installation and configuration, which n8n's own docs say require technical expertise, plus security and updates.
